source_refs.note: Chapter 6 exercise (PDF 135-138, printed 132-135), solved: MCQs keyed from the chapter (the book prints no key); short, constructed-response and comprehensive questions with model answers; numerical problems worked step by step and checked against the printed answers (6.1 and 6.2 corrected).

blocks.prompt: 6.1 In an isothermal change, internal energy:
blocks.explanation: In an isothermal process the temperature is constant. The internal energy of an ideal gas depends only on its temperature, so ΔU = 0 and Q = W (Section 6.4).

blocks.prompt: 6.2 First law of thermodynamics is based upon law of conservation of:
blocks.explanation: Q = ΔU + W: heat given to a system appears as increase in internal energy plus work done. This is the law of conservation of energy (Section 6.4).

blocks.prompt: 6.3 A device which converts mechanical energy into heat energy is called:
blocks.explanation: A heat engine (and a Carnot engine) changes heat into work, and a turbine gives mechanical work. A refrigerator works in reverse: work W is done on it and heat Q_H = Q_C + W is given out to the surroundings (Section 6.9).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: Strictly, a refrigerator does not "convert" mechanical energy into heat; it uses work to transfer heat from a cold body to a hot body (the work also ends up as heat given to the hot reservoir). Among the printed options, (c) is the intended answer.

blocks.prompt: 6.4 When two objects are made in thermal contact having same temperature, then they are at:
blocks.explanation: Bodies at the same temperature have no net heat flow between them, so they are in thermal equilibrium (Section 6.1).

blocks.prompt: 6.5 When the system is expanded by adding heat energy, then the work done will be:
blocks.explanation: An expanding gas pushes the piston out, so work is done by the system on its surroundings; by the sign convention this work is positive (W = PΔV with ΔV > 0).

blocks.prompt: 6.6 Entropy of a system in reversible process:
blocks.explanation: In a reversible process the entropy remains constant (Section 6.11), i.e., the change in entropy is zero. For irreversible processes it increases.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The book has no option "remains constant". What is zero in a reversible process is the change in total entropy (ΔS = 0), not the entropy itself; option (d) is taken in this sense.

blocks.prompt: 6.7 What happens to internal energy of an object when its temperature:
blocks.explanation: The internal energy of an ideal gas is directly proportional to its temperature (average K.E. = 3/2 k_B T), so a rise in temperature means an increase in internal energy (Section 6.2).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The question is printed incomplete ("when its temperature:"). It is read as "when its temperature increases", for which the internal energy increases (c).

blocks.prompt: 6.8 The value of Boltzmann constant is:
6.9 In an adiabatic process, there is no:
blocks.explanation: In an adiabatic process no heat enters or leaves the system (Q = 0), so W = −ΔU; the temperature does change.

blocks.prompt: 6.10 Thermodynamics mostly deals with:

options.text: Conversion of heat to other forms of energy

blocks.explanation: Thermodynamics is the branch of physics that deals with the relationships and conversions between heat and other forms of energy (Section 6.1).

blocks.prompt: 6.1 What is meant by thermal equilibrium? Explain briefly.
blocks.explanation:
Two bodies in thermal contact are in thermal equilibrium when they are at the same temperature, so there is no net flow of heat between them.
Example: a metal spoon in hot coffee takes heat until both reach the same temperature; then the heat flow stops.

blocks.prompt: 6.2 What is meant by internal energy? How is it related to temperature of an ideal gas?
blocks.explanation:
Internal energy is the sum of all molecular energies (kinetic and potential) of a substance.
In an ideal gas there are no intermolecular forces, so the internal energy is only the translational K.E. of the molecules. Since average K.E. = 3/2 k_B T, the internal energy of an ideal gas is directly proportional to its absolute temperature (U ∝ T).

blocks.prompt: 6.3 State 2nd law of thermodynamics in two different form.
blocks.explanation:
1. Kelvin's statement: it is impossible to devise a process which converts heat, extracted from a single reservoir, entirely into work without leaving any change in the working system.
2. In terms of entropy: if a system undergoes a natural process, it goes in the direction that causes the entropy of the system plus the environment to increase.
(Clausius's form, beyond the chapter's wording: heat cannot flow by itself from a colder body to a hotter body.)

blocks.prompt: 6.4 Is it possible to construct a heat engine of 100% efficiency? Explain.
blocks.explanation: No. Even an ideal Carnot engine has efficiency η = 1 − T₂/T₁, which is 100% only if the cold reservoir is at absolute zero (T₂ = 0 K), which is not available. By the second law (Kelvin), some heat must always be rejected to a cold sink; real engines also lose energy to friction.

blocks.prompt: 6.5 Differentiate between reversible and irreversible processes.
blocks.explanation: A reversible process can be retraced exactly in reverse; an irreversible process cannot.

rows: Can be retraced in exactly reverse order, without any change in the surroundings
Cannot be retraced backward by reversing the controlling factors
Working substance passes through the same stages; heat and work effects at each stage are exactly reversed
Stages are not repeated in reverse; effects are not reversed
Takes place very slowly (in equilibrium at every stage)
Takes place suddenly, or involves friction or heat loss
Entropy of system plus surroundings stays constant
Entropy of system plus surroundings increases
Examples: slow evaporation/liquefaction, slow compression of a gas
Examples: explosion, friction, mixing hot and cold water

blocks.prompt: 6.6 Why adiabate is steeper than isotherm? Explain.
blocks.explanation:
For an isotherm PV = constant, but for an adiabat PV^γ = constant, where γ > 1.
In adiabatic expansion no heat is supplied, so the gas does work from its internal energy and its temperature also falls. Thus for the same increase in volume the pressure falls more than in isothermal expansion (where temperature is kept constant), so the adiabatic curve is steeper.

blocks.prompt: 6.7 A refrigerator transforms heat from cold to hot body. Does this violate the second law of thermodynamics? Justify your answer.
blocks.explanation: No. The second law says heat cannot flow from a cold body to a hot body by itself. A refrigerator does not do it by itself: external work W (from the compressor, using electrical energy) is done on it, and the heat given to the hot surroundings is Q_H = Q_C + W. The entropy of the surroundings increases by more than the cold interior loses.

blocks.prompt: 6.8 Explain briefly heat death of universe in terms of entropy.
blocks.explanation: (The term is beyond the chapter; based on Section 6.11.) In every natural process the entropy of the universe increases and energy is degraded into thermal energy that cannot do work. Eventually the whole universe would reach the same temperature (maximum entropy); with no temperature difference, no heat could be changed into work and all processes would stop. This final state is called the heat death of the universe.

blocks.prompt: 6.9 Is it possible for a cyclic reversible heat engine to absorb heat at constant temperature and transforms it completely into work without rejecting some heat at low temperature? Explain.
blocks.explanation: No. By Kelvin's statement of the second law, heat from a single reservoir cannot be converted entirely into work in a cycle. A heat engine must work between a hot source and a cold sink and must reject some heat Q₂ to the sink, so W = Q₁ − Q₂ < Q₁ and η = 1 − T₂/T₁ < 1.

blocks.prompt: 6.10 How does behaviour of real gases differ from ideal gas at high pressure and low temperature? Identify the reasons behind these differences based on kinetic theory of gases.
blocks.explanation:
At high pressure and low temperature real gases do not obey PV = nRT; they deviate from ideal behaviour (they behave ideally only at low pressure and high temperature).
Reasons (kinetic theory assumptions fail): (i) the molecules come close together, so their own volume is no longer negligible compared with the container's volume; (ii) intermolecular attractive forces are no longer negligible, since slow molecules near each other attract, reducing the pressure on the walls.

blocks.prompt: 6.11 Show that area under P-V graph is equal to work done.
blocks.explanation:
Work done by a gas pushing a piston of area A through Δy at pressure P: W = FΔy = PAΔy = PΔV.
On a P-V graph at constant pressure, the area under the line between V₁ and V₂ is a rectangle of height P and width (V₂ − V₁) = ΔV, so area = PΔV = W. If P varies, the area is split into thin strips, each PΔV; their sum (the total area under the curve) is the total work.

blocks.prompt: 6.12 How is work done (i) by a gas (ii) on a gas? Calculate.
blocks.explanation:
Work is W = PΔV.
(i) By a gas: when the gas expands (ΔV > 0) and pushes the piston outward, it does work on the surroundings; W = PΔV is positive.
(ii) On a gas: when the gas is compressed by an external force (ΔV < 0), work is done on the gas; W = PΔV is negative.
Example: a gas expanding by 4.0 × 10⁻³ m³ at 8000 N m⁻² does W = 8000 × 4.0 × 10⁻³ = 32 J (Example 6.2).

blocks.prompt: 6.1 Explain how thermodynamics relates to the concept of energy conservation.
blocks.explanation:
The first law of thermodynamics, Q = ΔU + W, is the law of conservation of energy applied to heat and work: heat given to a system appears as an increase in its internal energy plus the work it does. Energy only changes form (e.g., chemical → thermal → mechanical); the total energy of an isolated system stays constant.
Examples:
• Isothermal process: ΔU = 0, so Q = W (all heat becomes work).
• Adiabatic process: Q = 0, so W = −ΔU (work comes from internal energy).
• Heat engine in a cycle: ΔU = 0, so W = Q₁ − Q₂.
• Bicycle pump: work done on the air raises its internal energy and temperature.
The law applies to all processes, including chemical, electrical and nuclear ones.

blocks.prompt: 6.2 Explain how thermodynamics applies to biological systems, such as human body.
blocks.explanation:
The energy-transforming processes in the body are called metabolism, and the first law applies to them: ΔU = Q − W.
• When we walk, run or move, the body does work W; energy is also needed for growth and to replace dead cells. This decreases the internal energy (stored chemical energy) of the body.
• The body also loses heat Q to the surroundings (sweating, breathing, radiation), which further lowers its internal energy.
• Food we eat supplies chemical energy that restores the internal energy and keeps the body temperature constant.
So energy is not created in the body; food energy is converted into work and heat. (Beyond the chapter: by the second law, the body keeps its ordered structure only by releasing heat that increases the entropy of the surroundings.)

blocks.prompt: 6.3 A gas is expanding adiabatically. Explain what happens to temperature and pressure of the the gas.
blocks.explanation:
In adiabatic expansion no heat enters or leaves (Q = 0), so by the first law W = −ΔU.
Temperature: the gas does work on the surroundings at the expense of its internal energy, so its internal energy decreases and its temperature falls.
Pressure: the pressure decreases, because the volume increases and the temperature also falls; it follows PV^γ = constant, so it falls faster than in an isothermal expansion (the adiabat is steeper).
Example: air rushing out of a burst tyre feels cold; rising air cools and forms clouds.

blocks.prompt: 6.4 A coffee cup is left on a table, and overtime coffee cup cools down. Explain thermodynamics processes occurring during this process.
blocks.explanation:
• Heat transfer: the coffee is hotter than its surroundings, so heat flows from the coffee to the cup, table and air by conduction, convection (rising warm air) and radiation; evaporation from the surface also carries heat away.
• First law: almost no work is done (W ≈ 0), so ΔU = Q; heat leaves (Q negative), the internal energy of the coffee decreases and its temperature falls.
• Second law and entropy: heat flows by itself only from hot to cold; this is an irreversible process. The coffee's entropy decreases (−Q/T_hot), but the surroundings gain more (+Q/T_cold), so the total entropy increases.
• Thermal equilibrium: cooling continues until the coffee reaches room temperature; then there is no net heat flow.

blocks.prompt: 6.5 How we can explain different weather patterns through thermodymical processes like wind, rain, etc.
blocks.explanation:
(Largely beyond the chapter; uses its ideas of heat transfer and adiabatic change.)
• Wind: the Sun heats land, sea and air unequally. Warm air expands, becomes less dense and rises (convection), leaving low pressure; cooler, denser air from high-pressure regions moves in to take its place. This flow of air is wind (e.g., sea breeze by day, land breeze by night).
• Clouds and rain: rising moist air expands adiabatically as the pressure falls with height, so its temperature falls (W = −ΔU). Water vapour condenses into droplets (clouds), releasing latent heat; when the droplets grow large enough they fall as rain (or snow/hail if cold enough). Cloud formation is an adiabatic process given in the chapter.
• Evaporation from seas absorbs heat and adds water vapour to the air, driving the water cycle.
Thus heat transfer, adiabatic expansion and changes of state together produce wind, clouds and rain.

blocks.prompt: 6.1 What are the postulates of kinetic theory of gases? Derive a relation for ideal gas equation in the form PV=NkT from general gas equation.
blocks.explanation:
Postulates of the kinetic theory of gases:
1. Gas molecules are in constant, random motion, moving in straight lines until they collide with each other or the walls.
2. The volume of the molecules is negligible compared with the volume of the gas (point masses).
3. There are no attractive or repulsive forces between the molecules, except during collisions.
4. Collisions between molecules and with the walls are perfectly elastic (no loss of K.E.).
5. A gas contains a very large number of molecules, so statistical methods can be used.
6. The average K.E. of the molecules is directly proportional to the absolute temperature.
7. The pressure of a gas is due to the collisions of its molecules with the walls.
8. The time of a collision is negligible compared with the time between collisions.

Derivation of PV = Nk_BT:
General (ideal) gas equation: PV = nRT ...(i)
The number of moles n = N/N_A, where N is the number of molecules and N_A = 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹ ...(ii)
Putting (ii) in (i): PV = (N/N_A)RT = N(R/N_A)T ...(iii)
The ratio R/N_A is the Boltzmann constant:
k_B = R/N_A = 8.3145/(6.02 × 10²³) = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J K⁻¹
So PV = Nk_BT
This is the ideal gas equation in terms of the Boltzmann constant.

blocks.prompt: 6.2 State and explain various gas laws.
blocks.explanation:
Gas laws relate pressure P, volume V and temperature T of a fixed mass of an ideal gas: one variable is kept constant while the other two change.

1. Boyle's law (1662): for a fixed mass of gas at constant temperature, the pressure varies inversely with the volume.
P ∝ 1/V, or PV = constant, or P₁V₁ = P₂V₂
Graph: P against V is a curve (hyperbola) falling from (P₁, V₁) to (P₂, V₂) (Fig. 6.1).

2. Charles' law: the volume of a given mass of gas at constant pressure is directly proportional to its absolute temperature.
V ∝ T, or V/T = constant, or V₁/T₁ = V₂/T₂
Graph: V against T is a straight line which, extended back, meets the temperature axis at −273 °C (0 K) (Fig. 6.2).

3. Gay-Lussac's law: for a fixed mass of gas at constant volume, the pressure varies directly with the absolute temperature.
P ∝ T, or P/T = constant, or P₁/T₁ = P₂/T₂
Graph: P against T is a straight line through the origin (Fig. 6.3).

Combining these laws gives the general (ideal) gas equation PV = nRT (R = 8.3145 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹), or PV = Nk_BT. Real gases obey these laws closely only at low pressure and high temperature.

blocks.prompt: 6.3 Explain first law of thermodynamics in detail. Give an example in support of your explanation. Give its two applications.
blocks.explanation:
Statement: in any thermodynamic process, when heat Q is added to a system, this energy appears as an increase in the internal energy ΔU stored in the system plus the work W done by the system on its surroundings.
Q = ΔU + W, or ΔU = Q − W
Explanation:
• When heat is added, the internal energy rises (temperature rises, pressure increases or state changes). If at the same time the gas expands, part of the heat is used to do work W = PΔV on the surroundings.
• Sign convention: heat entering the system +Q, heat leaving −Q; work done by the system +W, work done on the system −W.
• ΔU depends only on the initial and final states (internal energy is a state function).
• The first law is the law of conservation of energy: energy changes form but the total energy of an isolated system stays constant. It applies to all processes, including chemical, electrical and nuclear ones.

Example: a gas absorbs 42 J of heat and expands at 8000 N m⁻² through ΔV = 0.10 m² × 4.0 × 10⁻² m = 4.0 × 10⁻³ m³. W = PΔV = 32 J, so ΔU = Q − W = 42 J − 32 J = 10 J (Example 6.2). Another example: a bicycle pump becomes hot when pumped rapidly, because work done on the air raises its internal energy.

Applications:
1. Isothermal process (T constant): for an ideal gas ΔU = 0, so Q = W; all the heat supplied is used to do work (slow expansion).
2. Adiabatic process (no heat exchange): Q = 0, so W = −ΔU; in adiabatic expansion the gas cools (burst tyre, cloud formation), and in adiabatic compression it heats up.
(Also: human metabolism, ΔU = Q − W, where food restores the internal energy used for work and heat.)

blocks.prompt: 6.4 What is a refrigerator? Explain its working. Derive an expression for its co-efficient of performance.
blocks.explanation:
Refrigerator: a device which keeps the temperature of a body below that of its surroundings. It is a heat engine operating in reverse.

Working:
• It absorbs heat Q_C from the low-temperature reservoir (LTR, the inside compartment) and gives heat Q_H to the high-temperature reservoir (HTR, the surroundings).
• Heat does not flow from cold to hot by itself (Clausius statement of the second law), so external work W is done on the system by the compressor using electrical energy.
• (Beyond the chapter: a refrigerant liquid evaporates in the coils inside, absorbing heat; the compressor compresses the vapour, which condenses in the coils at the back and gives out heat to the room; it then expands back into the inside coils.)
• By energy conservation: Q_C + W = Q_H, or W = Q_H − Q_C
In a refrigerator work is done on the system, while in a heat engine work is done by the system.

Co-efficient of performance:
It is the ratio of the heat removed from the LTR (Q_C) to the work done (W):
E = Q_C/W
Using W = Q_H − Q_C:
E = Q_C/(Q_H − Q_C)
For an ideal refrigerator Q ∝ T (kelvin). With T₁ the cold and T₂ the hot temperature (book's notation):
E = T₁/(T₂ − T₁)
A better refrigerator removes more heat for less work, i.e., has a larger E. Example 6.4: E = 8 with T₁ = 250 K gives 8 = 250/(T₂ − 250), so T₂ = 281.25 K.

blocks.prompt: 6.5 What is Carnot engine? Describe Carnot cycle. State Carnot theorem and derive an expression for efficiency of Carnot engine.
blocks.explanation:
Carnot engine: an ideal heat engine, described by Sadi Carnot in 1824, that works in an ideal reversible cycle between two heat reservoirs using only isothermal and adiabatic processes. It is the most efficient possible engine.

Carnot cycle (ideal gas, P-V diagram ABCDA):
1. A→B, isothermal expansion at T₁: the gas absorbs heat Q₁ from the hot reservoir.
2. B→C, adiabatic expansion: the temperature falls from T₁ to T₂.
3. C→D, isothermal compression at T₂: the gas rejects heat Q₂ to the cold reservoir.
4. D→A, adiabatic compression: the gas returns to its initial state at T₁.
Thermal and mechanical equilibrium is maintained all the time, so each step is reversible. The net work in one cycle is the area enclosed by ABCDA.

Efficiency:
The gas returns to its initial state, so ΔU = 0. Net heat absorbed Q = Q₁ − Q₂. From the first law Q = ΔU + W:
W = Q₁ − Q₂
η = output work/input energy = W/Q₁
η = (Q₁ − Q₂)/Q₁ = 1 − Q₂/Q₁
In isothermal processes the heat transferred is proportional to the kelvin temperature, so Q₂/Q₁ = T₂/T₁:
η = 1 − T₂/T₁ = (T₁ − T₂)/T₁
Percentage efficiency = (1 − T₂/T₁) × 100
The efficiency depends only on the two temperatures, not on the working substance; it is 100% only if T₂ = 0 K, which is impossible. Example 6.3: T₁ = 700 K, T₂ = 350 K gives η = 50%.

Carnot's theorem: no heat engine can be more efficient than a Carnot engine operating between the same two temperatures. Extended: all Carnot engines operating between the same two temperatures have the same efficiency, irrespective of the working substance.

blocks.prompt: 6.5 Define and explain the term "Entropy".
blocks.explanation:
Definition: entropy S is a state variable (introduced by Clausius in 1856) that gives a quantitative basis to the second law. If a system absorbs heat ΔQ in a reversible process at absolute temperature T, its change in entropy is
ΔS = ΔQ/T (unit J K⁻¹)
Only the change in entropy is important, as with potential or internal energy.

Explanation:
• ΔS is positive when heat is added and negative when heat is removed.
• When heat Q flows from a reservoir at T₁ to one at T₂ (T₁ > T₂), the hot one loses Q/T₁ and the cold one gains Q/T₂. Since Q/T₂ > Q/T₁, the net change (Q/T₂ − Q/T₁) is positive. So in all natural processes the total entropy increases.
• Second law in terms of entropy: a natural process goes in the direction that causes the entropy of the system plus the environment to increase. For a reversible process the entropy stays constant; for an irreversible process it increases.
• Entropy and disorder: natural processes go towards greater disorder (heat flow from hot to cold, adding heat, free expansion of a gas), so entropy is a measure of molecular disorder.
• Degradation of energy: each increase in entropy means some energy is no longer available for work (e.g., mixed hot and cold water cannot be separated again). The entropy of the universe always increases.
Example 6.5: 1.0 kg ice melting at 0 °C: ΔS = mL_f/T = (1.0 × 3.36 × 10⁵)/273 = 1.23 × 10³ J K⁻¹.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The last two comprehensive questions are both numbered 6.5; the entropy question is the sixth question (6.6).

blocks.prompt: 6.1 A 2.5 g sample of an unknown gas is placed in a 25.0 L container at 300 K. The pressure of the gas is measured to be 8.21 atm. Calculate molar mass of unknown gas. (Ans: 37.6 g mol⁻¹)
blocks.explanation:
Given: m = 2.5 g, V = 25.0 L, T = 300 K, P = 8.21 atm, R = 0.0821 L atm mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ (= 8.3145 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹)
Required: molar mass M = ?
Formula: PV = nRT = (m/M)RT, so M = mRT/(PV)
Substitution: M = (2.5 g × 0.0821 L atm mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ × 300 K)/(8.21 atm × 25.0 L)
M = 61.575/205.25 g mol⁻¹
M = 0.300 g mol⁻¹
(In SI: P = 8.21 × 101,325 Pa = 8.32 × 10⁵ Pa, V = 0.025 m³; n = PV/RT = 8.34 mol; M = 2.5 g/8.34 mol = 0.300 g mol⁻¹.)
Answer: with the printed data, M = 0.300 g mol⁻¹.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The book prints 37.6 g mol⁻¹, which cannot be obtained from the printed data: 2.5 g, 25.0 L, 300 K and 8.21 atm give M = mRT/(PV) = 0.300 g mol⁻¹ (8.34 mol of gas). That is less than hydrogen (2 g mol⁻¹), so the printed data are inconsistent; 37.6 g mol⁻¹ would need a pressure of about 0.0655 atm (or a much larger mass).

blocks.prompt: 6.2 A gas occupies 6.0 L of volume at a pressure of 12 atm. What will be the volume of gas if the pressure is increased by 2.0 atm, assuming that temperature remains constant. (Ans: 3.6 L)
blocks.explanation:
Given: V₁ = 6.0 L, P₁ = 12 atm, pressure increased by 2.0 atm, so P₂ = 12 + 2.0 = 14 atm; T constant
Required: V₂ = ?
Formula (Boyle's law): P₁V₁ = P₂V₂, so V₂ = P₁V₁/P₂
Substitution: V₂ = (12 atm × 6.0 L)/14 atm
V₂ = 72/14 L
V₂ = 5.14 L
Answer: V₂ ≈ 5.1 L.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The book prints 3.6 L. Increasing 12 atm by 2.0 atm gives 14 atm and V₂ = 72/14 = 5.14 L. The printed 3.6 L is 72/20, i.e., it would need the pressure to be increased to 20 atm (by 8.0 atm).

blocks.prompt: 6.3 A gas undergoes a thermodynamic process where it absorbs 500 J of heat energy and performs 300 J work on its surroundings. Calculate the change in internal energy of the gas. (Ans: 200 J)
blocks.explanation:
Given: Q = +500 J (heat absorbed), W = +300 J (work done by the gas)
Required: ΔU = ?
Formula (first law): Q = ΔU + W, so ΔU = Q − W
Substitution: ΔU = 500 J − 300 J
ΔU = 200 J
Answer: the internal energy increases by 200 J (agrees with the book).

blocks.prompt:
6.4 A Carnot engine is operating between a high temperature reservoir at 600 K and a low temperature reservoir at 300 K. Calculate:
(i) the maximum possible efficiency
(ii) the amount of work output if the engine absorbs 500 J of heat from the high temperature reservoir. (Ans: 50%, 250 J)
blocks.explanation:
Given: T₁ = 600 K, T₂ = 300 K, Q₁ = 500 J
Required: (i) η = ? (ii) W = ?
(i) Formula: η = 1 − T₂/T₁
η = 1 − 300 K/600 K = 1 − 0.5 = 0.5
η = 0.5 × 100 = 50%
(ii) Formula: η = W/Q₁, so W = ηQ₁
W = 0.5 × 500 J
W = 250 J
(Heat rejected Q₂ = Q₁ − W = 250 J.)
Answer: (i) 50% (ii) 250 J (agrees with the book).

blocks.prompt:
6.5 A refrigerator extracts 1200 J of heat from its interior (the cold reservoir and releases 1800 J of heat to the surrounding environment) (the hot reservoir) during each cycle. Calculate:
(i) the work input required per cycle.
(ii) the co-efficient of performance (COP) of the refrigerator. (Ans: 600 J, 2)
blocks.explanation:
Given: Q_C = 1200 J, Q_H = 1800 J
Required: (i) W = ? (ii) E (COP) = ?
(i) Formula: Q_C + W = Q_H, so W = Q_H − Q_C
W = 1800 J − 1200 J
W = 600 J
(ii) Formula: E = Q_C/W
E = 1200 J/600 J
E = 2 (no unit)
Answer: (i) 600 J per cycle (ii) COP = 2 (agrees with the book).

blocks.prompt: 6.6 Calculate the entropy change when 1.0 mole of ice at 0 °C melts to form liquid water at the same temperature. (Ans: 22.0 J K⁻¹)
blocks.explanation:
Given: n = 1.0 mol of ice, molar mass of water = 18 g mol⁻¹, so m = 18 g = 0.018 kg
T = 0 °C = 273 K
Latent heat of fusion of ice L_f = 3.36 × 10⁵ J kg⁻¹ (as in Example 6.5)
Required: ΔS = ?
Formula: ΔS = ΔQ/T = mL_f/T
Heat absorbed: ΔQ = 0.018 kg × 3.36 × 10⁵ J kg⁻¹ = 6048 J
ΔS = 6048 J/273 K
ΔS = 22.2 J K⁻¹
Answer: ΔS ≈ 22.2 J K⁻¹ (the entropy increases). The book's 22.0 J K⁻¹ comes from the common value L_f = 3.33 × 10⁵ J kg⁻¹ (0.018 × 3.33 × 10⁵/273 = 21.96 ≈ 22.0 J K⁻¹).

blocks.prompt: 6.7 A gas occupies 400 mL at 20 °C. What volume will it occupy at 80 °C, assuming constant pressure? (Ans: 482 mL)
blocks.explanation:
Given: V₁ = 400 mL, T₁ = 20 °C = 20 + 273 = 293 K, T₂ = 80 °C = 80 + 273 = 353 K; pressure constant
Required: V₂ = ?
Formula (Charles' law): V₁/T₁ = V₂/T₂, so V₂ = V₁T₂/T₁
Substitution: V₂ = 400 mL × 353 K/293 K
V₂ = 400 × 1.205 mL
V₂ = 481.9 mL ≈ 482 mL
Answer: 482 mL (agrees with the book).

blocks.prompt: 6.8 A gas has a pressure of 2 atm at 300 K. What pressure will it have at 450 K, assuming constant volume? (Ans: 3 atm)
blocks.explanation:
Given: P₁ = 2 atm, T₁ = 300 K, T₂ = 450 K; volume constant
Required: P₂ = ?
Formula (Gay-Lussac's law): P₁/T₁ = P₂/T₂, so P₂ = P₁T₂/T₁
Substitution: P₂ = 2 atm × 450 K/300 K
P₂ = 2 × 1.5 atm
P₂ = 3 atm
Answer: 3 atm (agrees with the book).
